profile.name: Khorezm Lazgi
profile.tagline: A rhythmic, soul-stirring dance from the Khorezm region of Uzbekistan.
profile.insight: Legend says Lazgi was the divine music that first coaxed the human soul into a body of clay, causing the fingers, wrists, and elbows to stir with life for the very first time.
profile.profile: Khorezm Lazgi is a traditional dance and musical form from the Khorezm region of Uzbekistan, characterized by its rapid acceleration and intense, rhythmic energy. The dance follows a distinct structure, beginning with subtle, isolated movements of the extremities before evolving into a full-body performance. Recognized by UNESCO in 2019, it remains a central pillar of Khorezmian cultural identity.
profile.profile_long: Khorezm Lazgi is a traditional dance and musical form hailing from the Khorezm region of Uzbekistan. The dance is defined by its progressive intensity, beginning with slow, deliberate movements that gradually accelerate into a rapid, uncontrollable rhythm. According to oral tradition, the dance mimics the process of the soul entering a human body made of clay; the music is said to be the divine force that brought the limbs to life. The performance style varies by gender, with men portraying heroic and courageous themes, while women adopt a more lyrical and humorous approach. The dance is structured in three distinct parts following a short introduction, all performed in a 6/8 meter. As the music shifts, the dancer’s movements transition from isolated finger and wrist gestures to full-body engagement, ending abruptly as the tempo reaches its peak. In 2019, UNESCO inscribed the Khorezm dance Lazgi on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The form has been modernized and popularized by figures such as Komiljon Otaniyozov, who introduced new variations and instrumental styles in the mid-20th century. Today, the dance is celebrated through various regional styles, including Qayroq, Dutor, and Surnay Lazgi, each reflecting different musical accompaniments. It remains a vital part of the cultural landscape, with festivals held in the city of Khiva and global performances showcasing its unique, energetic character.

sections.origins_and_history: Oral traditions describe Lazgi as the divine music that allowed the soul to enter a body of clay. Historically, the dance has been preserved through the Khorezmian community and was formally recognized by UNESCO in 2019. In the 20th century, musicians like Komiljon Otaniyozov modernized the form by creating new instrumental and vocal variations.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance begins with slow, simple movements of the fingers, wrists, and elbows. As the music progresses, the dancer incorporates more complex movements of the feet and body. The performance is characterized by dancing on bent legs, shoulder movements, and the use of finger bells. The tempo increases throughout the performance, ending abruptly.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is composed of a short introduction followed by three distinct parts, played in a 6/8 meter. Instruments vary by the type of Lazgi, with specific styles named after instruments like the dutar, surnay, and garmon.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers often wear finger bells, which are fixed to the hands to accentuate the rhythmic movements of the wrists and fingers.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Lazgi serves as a cultural expression of Khorezmian identity. It is performed to demonstrate heroic and courageous traits in men and lyrical, humorous traits in women. It is also linked to the legend of the soul's creation.
sections.notable_figures: Tamara Khanum, Mukarrama Turgunbayeva, Gavhar Matyakubova, and Komiljon Otaniyozov are central figures in the development and global promotion of the dance.
sections.regional_variants: There are eight recognized types of Lazgi in Khorezm: Qayroq, Dutor, Surnay, Masxaraboz, Saroy, Changak, Khiva, and Garmon Lazgi.
sections.lineage: The dance has evolved from ancient oral traditions into a structured performance art, with modern yalla versions incorporating lyrics created by various 20th-century performers.

basic_steps: Engage full body on bent legs
teaching.level_notes: Beginners should focus on the slow, isolated movements of the extremities before attempting the faster, more intense full-body sequences.

claims.text: Lazgi was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on December 13, 2019.
claims.quote: Lazgi was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity under the name “Khorezm dance – Lazgi” on December 13, 2019.

claims.text: The dance is performed in a 6/8 meter and begins with slow movements of the fingers and wrists.
claims.quote: It is performed in a 6/8 meter with a lively rhythm. The dance starts with slow and simple movements; first the fingers, wrists, elbows and then the whole body comes to life.

claims.text: There are eight types of Lazgi dance in Khorezm.
claims.quote: There are 8 types of Lazgi dance in Khorezm: “Qayroq lazgi”, “Dutor lazgi”, “Surnay lazgi”, “Masxaraboz lazgi”, “Saroy lazgi”, “Changak lazgi”, “Khiva lazgi”, “Garmon lazgi”

claims.text: Dancers use finger bells during the performance.
claims.quote: Per questa danza è caratterizzata dal movimento sulle gambe piegate, spalle e agitando le mani con campane tintinnanti, fissate su di esse.
